paragraphs: Active learning lets a learning system choose which examples should receive labels. This paper combines that choice with an adaptive division of the input space. Instead of treating all inputs as one region, the algorithm constructs a finite collection of regions and seeks a separate predictor for each while continuing to request labels.

The central idea is to let the organization of the prediction problem change during learning. Choosing where to divide the input space and choosing which labels to acquire become parts of the same approach. This matters because a single predictor and a fixed regional division offer different degrees of flexibility; the proposed method makes regional adaptation an explicit component.

The authors prove guarantees for generalization error and label complexity, addressing both prediction on new examples and the number of labels needed. They also analyze the number of regions under mild assumptions. Experiments across several real-world datasets report substantial benefits over both single-region methods and region-based methods whose partitions do not adapt.
icml-2020-adaptive-region-based-active-l.tldr: An active learning algorithm adapts regional predictors and label requests together, with theoretical guarantees and reported gains on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Probabilistic forecasting models predict distributions over future values rather than just one value at each time step. This paper develops adversarial attacks against neural models that produce such sequences of distributions. The target includes autoregressive forecasting models that estimate future time-series behavior from the past.

The technical obstacle is computing how input changes affect statistics of the entire predicted sequence. Those statistics are estimated through Monte Carlo sampling, so an attack needs an effective way to differentiate through that estimation process. Addressing this obstacle allows the attack to work with quantities derived from the joint forecast distribution, rather than treating the forecast as a sequence of isolated point predictions.

The authors also extend probabilistic forecasting to a Bayesian setting that can condition on future observations as well as past ones. They demonstrate successful attacks using small input perturbations in stock trading and electricity-consumption prediction. These findings establish vulnerability in the studied tasks, where decisions depend on probabilistic forecasts, rather than asserting that every forecasting model behaves identically.
icml-2020-adversarial-attacks-on-probabi.tldr: The paper develops attacks on probabilistic sequence forecasts by differentiating through sampled distribution statistics and demonstrates vulnerabilities in two forecasting tasks.

paragraphs: Frank-Wolfe is an optimization method valued for its simplicity and for avoiding projection operations. Its progress can nevertheless be slow because the directions it chooses may be poor directions for reducing the objective. This paper targets that directional weakness while retaining the projection-free structure that makes the algorithm attractive.

The proposed method adds a subroutine that seeks a direction more closely aligned with the negative gradient. It does so in a matching-pursuit style: the subroutine progressively chases the desired direction rather than accepting the original direction unchanged. The contribution is therefore a way to improve the quality of the optimization step without giving up the defining computational property of Frank-Wolfe.

The authors derive convergence rates ranging from O(1/t) to O(exp(-ωt)). These describe different strengths of convergence established for the method, rather than one universal rate. Computational experiments report advantages over state-of-the-art alternatives both per iteration and in CPU time. Measuring both matters because better progress per iteration alone would not establish that the additional directional work pays off in elapsed computation.
icml-2020-boosting-frank-wolfe-by-chasin.tldr: A gradient-chasing subroutine improves Frank-Wolfe descent directions while preserving projection-free optimization, with convergence guarantees and computational gains.

paragraphs: A machine learning decision can affect both an immediate outcome and the environment in which later decisions occur. This makes fairness in lending, education, and recommendation a question about effects over time as well as effects at one moment. The paper develops causal directed acyclic graphs as a common framework for studying these interacting consequences.

The framework gives modelers a way to state and manipulate causal assumptions explicitly. Its emphasis is on interventional quantities: outcomes associated with changing how a system acts. That focus connects fairness questions to the effects of interventions on individuals and demographic groups, over both short and long horizons.

The authors explain two routes for evaluating these effects. When the environment's dynamics are known, causal assumptions enable simulation; when the dynamics are unknown, they enable estimation through adjustment. The contribution is a unified language for existing work and further investigation. Its conclusions depend on sound causal assumptions, making those assumptions part of the fairness analysis rather than leaving them implicit.
icml-2020-causal-modeling-for-fairness-i.tldr: Causal graphs organize fairness questions about interventions and their short- and long-term effects on individuals and groups.

paragraphs: Some scientific models can simulate observations even when their likelihood cannot be evaluated explicitly. This paper asks how to construct useful hypothesis tests and confidence regions in that setting. The challenge is to retain statistical validity and the ability to detect alternatives while relying on simulated data.

The proposed method, ACORE, recasts the likelihood-ratio test as a classification problem parameterized by the quantities being inferred. It then uses the relationship between tests and confidence sets to construct parameter regions. A separate goodness-of-fit procedure checks whether the resulting tests and confidence regions are valid, making validation an explicit part of the approach.

The method exploits the observation that relevant statistical quantities often vary smoothly with model parameters. Machine learning can therefore use simulations from nearby parameter settings to improve estimates, instead of relying only on simulations at one fixed setting. The authors provide theoretical and empirical support for this strategy. The claimed opportunity comes from sharing information across parameter values where that smoothness is available.
icml-2020-confidence-sets-and-hypothesis.tldr: ACORE uses classification and shared information across simulated parameter settings to build and check likelihood-free tests and confidence regions.

paragraphs: DINO is a Newton-type algorithm for optimizing an objective expressed as a finite sum across a distributed computing network. The paper focuses on communication efficiency as well as optimization behavior. Its guarantees allow arbitrary distributions of data across the network, making data placement an explicit part of the setting.

Under minimal assumptions, the authors establish global sublinear convergence to a first-order stationary point for general nonconvex functions. A stationary point is a point where the gradient vanishes; this guarantee does not by itself identify a global minimum. For objectives satisfying the Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality, they prove the stronger result of linear convergence.

The implementation uses linear least-squares subproblems, for which efficient solvers are available. The authors describe DINO as practically parameter free because it converges regardless of the selected hyperparameters within their stated framework, while still allowing easy tuning. Numerical simulations report efficiency relative to similar alternatives. Together, these results connect distributed convergence guarantees with subproblems designed to be straightforward to solve.
icml-2020-dino-distributed-newton-type-o.tldr: DINO combines communication-efficient distributed Newton-type optimization with stationary-point guarantees and linear convergence under the PL condition.

paragraphs: Double descent describes test error that rises near the point where a model can interpolate its training data, then falls with further overparameterization. This paper develops a quantitative explanation in the lazy learning regime, using high-dimensional random-features regression to study the phenomenon.

The authors derive an asymptotic bias-variance decomposition and separate variance due to dataset sampling, label noise, and weight initialization. Bias undergoes a transition at the interpolation threshold and stays constant beyond it. The label-noise and initialization contributions produce the peak near interpolation and the subsequent decline, identifying specific sources of the curve rather than attributing it to a single undifferentiated variance term.

The analysis also quantifies how averaging independently initialized estimators suppresses those contributions. In the limit of infinitely many estimators, test error decreases monotonically and becomes constant beyond interpolation. The paper compares ensembling, overparameterization, and regularization, then reports numerical experiments with qualitative agreement in realistic lazy learning scenarios. The theoretical explanation is thus tied to that regime, with experiments supporting its qualitative relevance there.
icml-2020-double-trouble-in-double-desce.tldr: A lazy-regime analysis attributes double descent to label-noise and initialization variance and quantifies how ensembling suppresses them.

paragraphs: Long-range planning requires searching through many possible action sequences to find a plan with multiple phases. Logical task-and-motion planners can narrow that search using action preconditions and effects, but those descriptions restrict flexibility in unfamiliar physical environments. Deep reinforcement learning offers flexible representations, yet sparse rewards make extended plans difficult to discover.

The Curious Sample Planner combines curiosity-guided sampling with imitation learning to accelerate planning. It brings together elements of task-and-motion planning and deep reinforcement learning, using exploration as part of the process for finding useful extended behavior. The authors also examine different curiosity measures and the kinds of solutions the planner discovers.

Across a range of physically realistic 3D tasks, the paper reports that the method efficiently finds complex, extended plans. Standard planning and learning methods often fail on these tasks or require very large and highly variable training samples. The authors further demonstrate task transfer: exploration policies learned on one task can improve efficiency on related tasks, allowing prior exploration experience to contribute to subsequent planning.
icml-2020-flexible-and-efficient-long-ra.tldr: The Curious Sample Planner combines curiosity-guided sampling and imitation learning to discover extended plans and transfer exploration experience across related tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether observed random graphs agree with a specified reference model. The reference is represented by a known symmetric matrix Q, while independent graph samples come from an unknown matrix P. The statistical task is to distinguish equality from a difference of at least a chosen size, measured using a matrix norm.

The setting is especially relevant when the number of graph samples is small relative to the graph's size. Different norms define different ways for a graph model to depart from the reference. The authors derive optimal minimax sample complexities for several natural choices, including the Frobenius and operator norms, characterizing the number of observations needed in the worst case.

They also turn test statistics into practical procedures using asymptotic distributions and parametric bootstrap calibration. Simulations compare these procedures and report improvements over baseline tests across several random graph models. The work therefore connects fundamental detection requirements with implementable tests, while keeping the definition of a detectable difference explicit through the selected norm.
icml-2020-goodness-of-fit-tests-for-inho.tldr: The paper derives optimal sample requirements and practical tests for detecting departures from a known random-graph model.

paragraphs: Time-series representations often use a bank of filters to reveal signal structure across time and frequency. This paper proposes learning such filter banks through a Group Transform framework. The framework generalizes classical constructions such as the wavelet transform while allowing the representation to adapt to the signal and task.

A wavelet filter bank is constructed through affine transformations of a mother filter. The proposed approach admits nonlinear transformations instead, expanding the available representations to include wavelet and chirplet-like filters. The authors parameterize the nonlinear map so that its sampling can be optimized, making the transform's construction part of learning rather than a wholly fixed preprocessing choice.

The Learnable Group Transform can be expressed as a deep neural network. Experiments on diverse time-series datasets demonstrate the framework's expressive capacity and report performance competitive with state-of-the-art approaches. The significance is the combination of a structured signal-transform perspective with learnable nonlinear variation, providing a broader family of representations without claiming that one fixed transform suits every signal.
icml-2020-learnable-group-transform-for-.tldr: Learnable Group Transforms extend wavelet-style filter banks with nonlinear transformations that can adapt to a time-series task.

paragraphs: Testing a classifier's adversarial robustness often means searching for an input change that alters its prediction. Exact robustness computation does not scale well to large networks, so empirical attacks play a central role. This paper proposes a white-box attack aimed at finding a small perturbation sufficient to change an input's class.

The attack supports the l1, l2, and l-infinity norms, which provide different measures of perturbation size. It has a geometric interpretation and directly seeks to reduce distortion. Finding small perturbations is useful beyond testing one fixed budget: the results of a single run can be used to evaluate attack-based robust accuracy across perturbation thresholds.

The authors report that the method quickly produces high-quality results and performs similarly to or better than state-of-the-art attacks, including methods partly specialized to individual norms. They also report robustness to gradient obfuscation. These findings concern the effectiveness of the empirical search; the stated aim of minimizing distortion should not be read as a guarantee that every returned perturbation is the exact smallest possible one.
icml-2020-minimally-distorted-adversaria.tldr: A geometric white-box attack searches efficiently for small class-changing perturbations across three norms and supports evaluation at multiple thresholds.

paragraphs: This paper studies normalized stochastic gradient descent, focusing on how momentum changes its convergence behavior on nonconvex objectives. The authors provide an improved analysis showing that adding momentum removes the need for large batch sizes. The result gives theoretical support to a modification of the optimizer rather than simply reporting a favorable training curve.

For objectives with bounded second derivative, a small change to the momentum formula yields an O(1/epsilon^3.5) iteration bound for reaching an epsilon-critical point. This is a point with a sufficiently small gradient, rather than necessarily a global optimum. The bound matches the best-known rates described in the paper without logarithmic factors or dependence on dimension.

The authors also introduce an adaptive learning-rate schedule whose convergence rate improves automatically when gradient variance is small. Experiments on ResNet-50 and BERT pretraining show performance matching the different methods used to obtain state-of-the-art results on those tasks. Together, the results connect momentum's theoretical benefit with effectiveness across two distinct large-scale learning applications.
icml-2020-momentum-improves-normalized-s.tldr: Momentum strengthens normalized SGD's convergence guarantees, removes a large-batch requirement, and performs effectively on ResNet-50 and BERT pretraining.

paragraphs: In online learning with partial information, a learner does not necessarily observe every action's loss. A feedback graph describes which losses become visible. This paper studies a setting where those graphs change randomly over time and, crucially, are statistically dependent on the losses themselves.

That dependence makes the feedback mechanism part of the learning problem: which information is observed is connected to the outcomes being learned about. The authors motivate the setting through applications with correlated action outcomes. They design an algorithm that uses the stochastic properties of the feedback graphs, rather than treating the pattern of observations as unrelated to the losses.

The paper provides a detailed theoretical analysis and favorable regret guarantees, which assess accumulated performance relative to a comparison benchmark. Experiments on real-world datasets also report improvements over standard algorithms for learning with feedback graphs. The contribution is to handle a more interconnected observation process while retaining theoretical control, with empirical evidence supporting the approach in the evaluated settings.
icml-2020-online-learning-with-dependent.tldr: A new online learning algorithm exploits randomly changing feedback graphs even when the graphs and observed losses are dependent.

paragraphs: Online learning algorithms can adapt in several distinct senses. They may adjust to the scale of observed gradients, perform well over short intervals, or compete with a reference decision that changes over time. This paper presents one algorithm that combines these forms of adaptivity in its regret guarantees.

Its parameter-free bound adapts to the comparator's norm and the squared sizes of observed gradients. Its strongly adaptive guarantee controls regret on any interval of length N at a rate of approximately square root N, suppressing logarithmic factors. This interval-level guarantee addresses performance within portions of the sequence, rather than only a bound over the entire learning history.

The algorithm also achieves an optimal dynamic regret bound expressed as approximately square root of PN, again suppressing logarithmic factors, for comparator sequences with path length P. Path length measures how much the comparator changes. The central technical contribution is a method for combining constrained online-learning bounds without an expert meta-algorithm, allowing the different guarantees to coexist within a single approach.
icml-2020-parameter-free-dynamic-and-str.tldr: One online learning algorithm combines scale-sensitive, interval-wise, and changing-comparator regret guarantees through a new way of combining bounds.

paragraphs: Change-point detection seeks to identify when the distribution generating a data stream changes. In applications involving hospital records or activity inside a home, detecting a shift must also respect the sensitivity of individual observations. This paper develops detection algorithms with differential privacy guarantees for settings where the underlying distributions are unknown.

The unknown-distribution setting is central to the contribution. Much prior work described in the abstract, including the existing private methods, assumes complete knowledge of the distributions before and after a change. Removing that requirement addresses situations where the detector must work without being given both sides of the transition in advance.

The proposed setting also allows distributions to evolve smoothly over time, rather than remaining fixed on either side of a single abrupt change. The authors apply their algorithms to detecting changes in linear trends and provide experiments validating their performance. The work thus broadens private change detection along two dimensions: incomplete distributional knowledge and streams whose ordinary behavior can itself vary over time.
icml-2020-privately-detecting-changes-in.tldr: The paper develops differentially private change detectors for unknown distributions, including streams with smoothly evolving behavior and changing linear trends.

paragraphs: Predictive agents can learn internal representations of their surroundings, but interpreting those representations directly is difficult. This paper proposes asking questions as a way to reveal what they contain. The authors study agents trained with action-conditional CPC and SimCore in a visually rich 3D environment containing varied objects, properties, and spatial arrangements.

After predictive training, a decoder answers synthetic English questions using each agent's internal state. Gradients from this question-answering decoder are not passed back into the agent. That separation matters because the probe examines information acquired through predictive learning, rather than teaching the agent to encode answers through the questioning objective.

The agents' answers indicate that their representations encode factual and seemingly compositional information about objects, attributes, quantities, and spatial relations. The qualification about compositionality remains important: the findings suggest this structure rather than establishing unrestricted compositional understanding. Question-based probing makes the results human-interpretable and is designed to apply across modeling approaches, potentially informing the development of stronger predictive objectives.
icml-2020-probing-emergent-semantics-in-.tldr: Question-answering probes reveal factual and seemingly compositional environmental information in predictive agents without training the agents through the probe.

paragraphs: R2-B2 combines Bayesian optimization with recursive reasoning in repeated games. It addresses agents whose payoff functions are unknown, complex, and expensive to evaluate. Recursive reasoning models how an agent accounts for other agents' reasoning while making its own decisions, with the agents treated as boundedly rational and self-interested.

The framework does not impose a particular relationship between different agents' payoffs. It can therefore cover constant-sum, general-sum, and common-payoff games. The authors prove faster asymptotic convergence to no regret than without recursive reasoning when an agent reasons at level two or higher and exactly one level above the other agents. The improvement is conditional on that reasoning relationship.

A cheaper variant, R2-B2-Lite, reduces computation at the cost of a weaker convergence guarantee. Experiments involving synthetic games, adversarial machine learning, and multi-agent reinforcement learning demonstrate the method's performance and breadth. The paper thus connects strategic reasoning depth with learning efficiency, while making the tradeoff between computational cost and theoretical guarantees explicit.
icml-2020-r2-b2-recursive-reasoning-base.tldr: R2-B2 combines recursive reasoning and Bayesian optimization, proving faster no-regret convergence under a specific advantage in reasoning depth.

paragraphs: Online advertising auctions generate data at an extremely high rate. Sellers seeking to maximize revenue must learn monopoly prices while auctions continue to arrive. The paper focuses on the computational requirement this creates: each learning update must remain fast enough to keep pace with the stream.

The abstract identifies a scaling problem in existing methods inherited from batch learning. Their time and memory requirements per update grow as O(square root t), where t tracks the stream's progression. Even growth slower than linear can become burdensome when the volume of observations is enormous, so the cost of each successive update matters independently of the pricing objective itself.

The authors present what they describe as the first algorithm for online monopoly-price learning in auctions with constant time and memory per update. This means the stated update cost does not increase with t. The main result addresses the feasibility of sustained real-time learning: it changes the computational scaling of price updates rather than reporting a particular numerical revenue improvement.
icml-2020-real-time-optimisation-for-onl.tldr: The paper introduces online monopoly-price learning with constant time and memory per update for high-frequency auctions.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows model distributions using invertible transformations. This paper identifies a structural difficulty when the target distribution's support has complicated topology. The authors prove that, in the studied scenario, closely approximating the target forces a flow toward arbitrarily severe numerical noninvertibility.

The result distinguishes mathematical invertibility from usable numerical behavior. A transformation can be constrained to remain a bijection while becoming increasingly problematic to invert numerically. The issue has implications for flow models generally and is especially relevant to residual flows, which explicitly control the Lipschitz constant of their bijection.

To address the problem, the authors introduce continuously indexed flows, replacing a single bijection with a continuously indexed family. Intuitively, this added flexibility can correct probability mass that one bijection would place incorrectly. They show theoretically that the resulting models avoid the same topological limitations and report improved empirical performance across several models and benchmarks. The contribution connects a precise representational obstacle to an architectural change designed to remove it.
icml-2020-relaxing-bijectivity-constrain.tldr: Continuously indexed flows replace a single bijection with a family of bijections to avoid identified topological limitations of normalizing flows.

paragraphs: A defense can appear robust when the attack used to evaluate it is poorly configured or hindered by misleading gradients. This paper treats reliable attack evaluation as a prerequisite for measuring progress in adversarial defenses. It focuses on failures involving attack hyperparameters, gradient masking, and the attack's objective function.

The authors introduce two extensions of projected gradient descent attacks that address suboptimal step sizes and objective-function problems. They combine these with two complementary existing attacks into a parameter-free ensemble. The resulting evaluation is designed to be computationally affordable and independent of user-specific tuning choices, reducing opportunities for evaluation outcomes to hinge on those choices.

The ensemble is applied to more than 50 published models. In every case except one, it finds lower robust test accuracy than originally reported, often by more than 10%, and identifies several broken defenses. These results show that the tested defenses were frequently less robust than their reported evaluations suggested. The ensemble provides a stronger empirical assessment, rather than an exact certificate of robustness.
icml-2020-reliable-evaluation-of-adversa.tldr: A parameter-free ensemble of complementary attacks exposes overstated robustness in nearly all of more than 50 evaluated models.

paragraphs: Generating a graph by constructing its full adjacency matrix requires considering a number of entries quadratic in the node count. That becomes expensive even when the graph contains relatively few edges. This paper introduces BiGG, an autoregressive generative model designed to exploit that common sparsity.

For a graph with n nodes and m edges, BiGG avoids generating the full adjacency matrix and achieves O((n + m) log n) generation time. The advantage is tied to graphs where m is much smaller than n squared. The model also supports parallel training with O(log n) synchronization stages, compared with the at-least-linear number required by the autoregressive alternatives discussed in the abstract.

Experiments across several benchmarks report generation of graphs orders of magnitude larger than previously possible with deep autoregressive graph models, alongside better generation quality. The contribution therefore addresses both the amount of work needed to represent sparse structure and the sequential coordination needed during training. The empirical findings indicate that the scaling improvement did not require sacrificing quality on the evaluated benchmarks.
icml-2020-scalable-deep-generative-model.tldr: BiGG exploits graph sparsity to reduce generation cost and training synchronization while improving benchmark scale and generation quality.

paragraphs: This paper studies the statistical limits of adversarially robust classification under a Gaussian mixture model. Its focus is excess risk: how far a learned classifier's risk lies above the optimal risk in the setting. The aim is to characterize the best achievable learning accuracy, rather than only propose another defense.

The authors express their results using an adversarial signal-to-noise ratio, or AdvSNR. This quantity extends the corresponding concept from ordinary linear classification to account for adversarial perturbations. For AdvSNR r, the stated optimal rate has the form exp(-(1/2 + o(1))r squared) multiplied by d/n, linking the guarantee to signal strength, dimension, and sample count.

They prove a minimax lower bound and construct a computationally efficient estimator attaining the optimal rate. Matching these establishes both a worst-case statistical barrier and an achievable procedure within the Gaussian-mixture setting. The results require minimal assumptions as described by the authors and cover a broad range of perturbations, including lp balls for every p at least one.
icml-2020-sharp-statistical-guaratees-fo.tldr: For Gaussian-mixture classification, the paper matches optimal robust excess-risk bounds with an efficient estimator using adversarial signal-to-noise ratio.

paragraphs: This paper examines how supervision and structural constraints affect generalization in linear subspace fitting. It studies an overparameterized setting where the fitted subspace can perfectly interpolate the training examples. The question is how test behavior changes when the learning problem moves between unsupervised subspace estimation and supervised regression.

The authors define a family of least-squares problems using two adjustable properties. One is the proportion of training examples that provide input-output supervision for the desired low-dimensional mapping. The other is how strictly the learned operator's defining vectors must be orthonormal. Together, these properties form a plane of problem settings rather than a single fixed estimation task.

At one end lies standard unsupervised fitting with strict orthonormality; at another lies fully supervised regression without structural constraints on the operator. Exploring the intermediate settings, the authors find double-descent trends as supervision increases and orthonormality constraints weaken. The result connects generalization behavior to the formulation of the learning problem, showing how changing these two properties accompanies the emergence of double descent.
icml-2020-subspace-fitting-meets-regress.tldr: A continuum from subspace fitting to regression reveals double-descent trends as supervision increases and orthonormality constraints weaken.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix factorization compresses a data matrix into a smaller representation. Before fitting it, practitioners often normalize features to address outliers and differences in scale. This paper makes normalization part of the optimization problem, learning it jointly with the factorization instead of fixing it through a separate preprocessing rule.

The method learns parameters of quantile-normalization operators that act row by row on the original feature matrix, its low-rank reconstruction, or both. The objective is to improve the quality of the resulting low-rank representation. This couples the transformation of feature values to the representation being fitted, so the normalization is chosen in relation to the factorization task.

The technical ingredient is a differentiable quantile-normalization operator built using optimal transport. Differentiability facilitates joint optimization of the normalization parameters and the factorization. The authors demonstrate applicability on synthetic and genomics datasets. The contribution is both a learnable alternative to ad hoc preprocessing and an operator that makes such coordinated learning possible within the proposed optimization framework.
icml-2020-supervised-quantile-normalizat.tldr: A differentiable optimal-transport operator lets quantile normalization be learned jointly with low-rank matrix factorization.

paragraphs: Posterior collapse occurs when a variational autoencoder's latent posterior becomes an uninformative prior. Although some narrow asymptotic settings give Gaussian VAEs favorable global optima, training can still produce poor solutions. This paper investigates the role of bad local minima in explaining that gap between an available optimum and an obtained model.

The authors argue that collapse is at least partly a property of the loss surface of deep autoencoders, beyond explanations centered on excessive KL-divergence regularization. They prove that even small nonlinear changes to affine VAE decoders can create problematic local minima. Thus, introducing nonlinearity can alter the optimization landscape in a way directly relevant to collapse.

For deeper models, analogous minima can make a VAE act like a severe truncation operation, discarding information across every latent dimension under certain circumstances. These are conditional results, not a claim that all nonlinear VAEs must collapse. The paper adds an optimization-landscape explanation to existing accounts, identifying an additional risk factor while explicitly preserving the value of other explanations.
icml-2020-the-usual-suspects-reassessing.tldr: The paper shows that nonlinear VAE loss landscapes can contain local minima that cause posterior collapse, adding to existing explanations.
